Bread dough rises because yeast consumes sugars and produces carbon dioxide gas. A developed gluten network in the dough traps that gas. As the gas builds up, it expands the dough, helping it grow in volume.

Temperature affects how quickly this happens. Within normal proofing temperatures, warmth generally makes yeast more active, so dough rises faster. In cooler conditions, yeast works more slowly. A cool rise takes longer, but that extra time can allow more flavor to develop. A warmer rise can be useful when you want the dough ready sooner, though hotter is not always better: excessive heat can damage or kill the yeast.

Leaving dough to proof for too long can also cause problems. Its structure may weaken until it can no longer hold the gas well. The dough can then lose gas and collapse. Because recipes and conditions vary, watch the dough’s expansion and texture rather than relying only on a fixed time.
